Triple-Zero Roulette: How a Third Pocket Raises the House Edge

Published October 12, 2026 · 8 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Most players learn the roulette house-edge story in one sentence: European wheels have a single zero, American wheels bolt on a second one, and the extra pocket roughly doubles the house's cut. That comparison covers the two wheels you'll find on the overwhelming majority of casino floors. It doesn't cover a newer variant that's shown up at a smaller number of US casinos in recent years — one that adds a third non-paying pocket to the layout and pushes the math further than either of the familiar wheels does.

In this guide

  1. What triple-zero roulette actually is
  2. The math: how the house edge changes
  3. Comparing all three wheels side by side
  4. Why a casino would offer a worse wheel

What triple-zero roulette actually is

A standard European wheel has 37 pockets: the numbers 1 through 36, plus a single green 0. A standard American wheel has 38 pockets: the same 1 through 36, plus both a 0 and a 00. Triple-zero roulette takes that same American layout and adds one more non-paying green pocket, usually labeled 000, bringing the total to 39 pockets. The numbered pockets — 1 through 36, with their usual odd/even and red/black coloring — work exactly the same as on any other wheel. The only change is that there are now three green pockets instead of one or two, and all three lose for every standard inside and outside bet, the same way 0 and 00 already do on an American wheel.

From across the pit, a triple-zero wheel can look deceptively close to an ordinary American one — same numbers, same betting layout, same chip denominations. The difference is entirely in that extra green pocket, which is exactly why it's worth knowing how to spot before you place a bet.

The math: how the house edge changes

House edge on a wheel-based game comes down to one simple comparison: how often a bet actually wins versus what it pays when it does. Take a straight-up bet on a single number, which pays 35 to 1 on every version of roulette. On a European wheel, that number is one of 37 pockets, so the true odds against it are 36 to 1 — the house is paying 35 when it should mathematically pay 36, and that one-unit gap is where the edge comes from, working out to about 2.70%. On an American wheel, the same bet is one of 38 pockets, pushing the edge to about 5.26%. Add the third zero and that same bet is now one of 39 pockets while still paying 35 to 1 — and the edge rises again, to roughly 7.69%.

Even-money bets follow the identical pattern, just with different numbers. Red/black, odd/even, and high/low each cover 18 of the wheel's numbered pockets and pay even money. On a 38-pocket American wheel, your actual win probability is 18/38, which works out to that same 5.26% edge once you compare it to a fair coin-flip payout. On a 39-pocket triple-zero wheel, your win probability drops to 18/39 — and the edge climbs to 7.69% there too. Every bet on the layout, inside and outside alike, picks up roughly the same 2.4-percentage-point tax versus the American wheel, because the extra pocket doesn't help any bet in any way — it simply adds one more losing outcome to the denominator of every single wager.

Takeaway: Going from a European wheel to a triple-zero wheel very roughly triples the house's cut on every bet on the table — from about 2.70% to about 7.69% — without changing a single payout number on the felt.

Comparing all three wheels side by side

European (single-zero)American (double-zero)Triple-zero
Total pockets373839
Non-paying green pockets1 (0)2 (0, 00)3 (0, 00, 000)
Straight-up bet payout35 to 135 to 135 to 1
House edge, most bets~2.70%~5.26%~7.69%
Expected loss per $100 wagered, long run~$2.70~$5.26~$7.69

That last row is the number worth sitting with. On otherwise identical betting patterns, a triple-zero wheel costs you close to three times what a European wheel does over the long run, and almost half again more than an American wheel — all from a single extra pocket that doesn't change how any individual bet is marked up on the felt.

Why a casino would offer a worse wheel

Triple-zero roulette isn't a mistake or an oversight — it's a deliberate product, and casinos have a straightforward business reason to offer it: a worse house edge on the base game generates more revenue per hour of play without requiring any change to minimum bets, table limits, or dealer pace. Some versions are also bundled with bonus payouts tied specifically to the extra pocket — for instance, a side bet or a boosted payout if the ball lands on 000 — which gives the casino a marketing hook ("a third zero means a third way to win something extra") that can make the wheel feel novel rather than simply worse. The core math doesn't change regardless of how the bonus feature is framed: three non-paying pockets instead of one or two is strictly worse for every standard bet on the layout.

This isn't unique to roulette. Side bets with inflated house edges, novelty wheel variants, and bonus-feature overlays show up across the casino floor as a way to add variety and marketing appeal on top of a base game, often at the cost of a notably worse edge than the plain version of the same game. If you're interested in that pattern more broadly, our guide on house edge across different casino games covers where the best and worst odds tend to sit.

How to spot a triple-zero wheel before you sit down

On a physical table, the fastest check is simply counting the green pockets on the wheel itself, or checking the felt layout for a marked 000 box, which sits alongside the 0 and 00 boxes rather than hidden anywhere subtle. Some casinos post the wheel type or house-edge information on a table placard; when that information isn't posted, asking the dealer directly is a fair and common question. Online, the game's name is usually explicit — look for "Triple Zero," "000," or similar wording in the game title or lobby description, and check the posted RTP or house-edge figure in the game's info/paytable screen before you load a single spin, since legitimate online casinos are required to disclose this.

If you've already found and compared tables, the practical rule holds regardless of format: an American double-zero wheel is the common default in most US casinos, a European single-zero wheel is the better find when available, and a triple-zero wheel is worth avoiding unless the specific promotion or bonus feature meaningfully offsets the higher baseline cost — which, for most bet sizes and session lengths, it doesn't. For the fuller rundown on how the standard wheels differ, see our roulette basics guide, and for how zero-cutting rules can improve a European wheel even further, see our piece on la partage and en prison.

Frequently asked questions

Is triple-zero roulette common in US casinos?

No. It's a niche variant found at a relatively small number of properties rather than a standard offering, while American double-zero wheels remain the default at most US casino floors.

Does the third zero pay out differently than 0 and 00?

On the standard bets, no — 000 loses for every inside and outside bet exactly like 0 and 00 do. Some versions pair the wheel with a separate bonus bet tied specifically to landing on 000, but that's an additional side wager, not a change to how the core bets resolve.

Does adding a third zero affect every bet on the table equally?

Yes. Because the extra pocket is simply one more losing outcome added to the total, it raises the house edge by roughly the same amount — about 2.4 percentage points relative to the American wheel — across every standard inside and outside bet.

How can I tell if an online roulette game uses a triple-zero wheel?

Check the game's title and its posted RTP or house-edge figure in the paytable or info screen. A house edge noticeably above the standard 5.26% American figure, or wording like "Triple Zero" in the title, is the giveaway.
